title: Clarity, centre and conventions: safeguarding the UK constitution
label: 11 November 2026 · Constitutional safeguards
summary: Morgan McSweeney, former chief of staff to the Prime Minister, told the Constitution Committee that the UK’s constitution faces two distinct pressures—abuse of power and government failure to deliver—and that many current problems come from an accumulation of unclear rules and precedents. He urged a parliamentary-led review to reduce and clarify rules (possibly by codifying the Cabinet Manual), to fix how cross-department decisions are handled, to strengthen strategic capacity at the centre of government, and to preserve but clarify the roles of Parliament, courts, Cabinet and the Civil Service.

chapters.title: Two different threats
chapters.takeaway: Constitutional risk comes from both abuse of power and government failure to deliver; both can undermine legitimacy.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Do you think the UK’s constitutional democracy is under threat, and what did you see in No. 10?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: There are always pressures. Two ways a constitution is threatened: abuse of power, and Governments failing to deliver their lawful programmes. Populists exploit the latter. Both can erode legitimacy.

turns.speaker: Lord Murphy of Torfaen
turns.text: Would you want changes to the UK constitution?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: Yes. There are many rules shaping Prime Ministerial power. Individually they often made sense, but together they form a thicket. We should identify fewer, justified rules and consider codifying the essentials—like the Cabinet Manual—so roles are clearer.

chapters.title: Who should decide changes — and why clarity matters
chapters.takeaway: Reform should be driven by Parliament, not the Prime Minister, and clarity stops inconsistent interpretations that slow government.

turns.speaker: Lord Murphy of Torfaen
turns.text: Could the Ministerial Code be made statutory?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: Possibly. But first do a wider review of accumulated rules. Many were added after mistakes; they now work by precedent. Parliament should lead any codification so it’s not just the Prime Minister deciding.

turns.speaker: Lord Beith
turns.text: What if a Prime Minister says delivery is urgent and overrides other safeguards?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: There are safeguards—courts, Parliament, Cabinet, civil servants, parties, elections. They should remain. But we need clarity so Prime Ministers know the limits of their power and won’t rough-guess based on different civil‑service interpretations.

turns.speaker: Lord Griffiths of Burry Port
turns.text: How do you ensure leaders have the character and judgment to respect conventions?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: Codes can't guarantee character. Parties play a role—choosing candidates and leaders—and voters ultimately judge. We can only make the rules clear and robust enough to constrain abuse.

chapters.title: Quasi-judicial decisions and Secretary of State autonomy
chapters.takeaway: Some laws interpreted to mean a single Secretary of State must decide can stop necessary Cabinet discussion; fix interpretation, not always the law.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: You mentioned judicial review earlier; do you think courts intervene too much?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: I misspoke. My concern is 'quasi-judicial processes'—laws that say 'the Secretary of State shall decide' and which are interpreted to prevent Cabinet-level consultation. That interpretation can block timely, cross-department discussion.

turns.speaker: Lord Jones of Penybont
turns.text: So what do you want changed—the law or its practice?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: Often the law's application or precedent causes the problem. I wouldn't remove Secretary of State decision-making where statute requires it. But where decisions affect many departments, there should be a clear route for Cabinet or PM input while preserving the Secretary of State's formal role.

turns.speaker: Lord Beith
turns.text: Is the autonomy of Secretaries of State part of the constitution or just practice?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: Where statute names the Secretary of State, that should stand. The reform needed is clearer rules about consultation and when collective discussion is appropriate, especially for national-security or economy-wide matters.

chapters.title: Civil Service role and the centre of government
chapters.takeaway: The Civil Service should protect the constitution and advise on legality; the centre needs more strategic cohesion and coordination.

turns.speaker: Lord Bichard
turns.text: Should civil servants act to protect the constitution beyond advising Ministers?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: They should and largely do. But distinguish two cases: if a civil servant thinks a Minister is acting unlawfully, different routes are needed than when a civil servant thinks a Minister is ignoring convention.

turns.speaker: Lord Bichard
turns.text: So civil servants might resist implementing political wishes to defend constitutional principles?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: Yes, if the action is unlawful. When it’s a matter of changing precedent or convention, civil servants must implement lawful decisions—even if they disagree—while flagging risks and using informal channels to resolve disputes first.

turns.speaker: Lord Waldegrave of North Hill
turns.text: You said the centre of government is 'too weak'—how would you strengthen it?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: Size isn’t the same as strength. The centre needs coherent coordination: strategic capacity that plans ahead for things like Budgets and King's Speeches, and better coordination of communications and cross-department delivery, not more fragmented teams.

turns.speaker: Lord Waldegrave of North Hill
turns.text: So more central strategy and joined-up teams, not just more staff?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: Exactly. Clear priorities from the Prime Minister, routed through a stronger centre that can chase departments and produce consistent action.

chapters.title: Parliament, parties and practical checks
chapters.takeaway: Parliament, parties and political reality are essential checks; reforms should come from Parliament and MPs remain capable of holding government to account.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: Can the Commons act as a restraint when interpretations go against Parliament’s intent?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: Yes. Parliament can amend bad legislation, use PMQs, committees, or pass new laws. It should be central to deciding which rules stay, which change, and to any codification.

turns.speaker: Lord Cryer
turns.text: But haven't both Cabinet and Commons become weaker over decades?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: My experience is MPs are well informed and engaged on national issues. Cabinets still include strong figures who will push back. No single check is perfect—courts, Parliament, Cabinet, civil servants and parties all matter together.

turns.speaker: Lord Beith
turns.text: Who should lead the review of accumulated rules?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: Parliament should lead it—committees like this can recommend. The Prime Minister shouldn’t alone rewrite conventions; that risks politicising rules that protect the constitution.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Any final practical example of change you’d press for?

turns.speaker: Morgan McSweeney
turns.text: Review quasi‑judicial interpretations to allow necessary Cabinet input; codify core roles in the Cabinet Manual so everyone—Ministers, civil servants and the public—knows who decides what and when.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you for your time and for joining us from Chicago this morning.
